Question: Can a truck with a very high lift and large tires for example on an f350 be towed or is it dangerous that towing companies wont do it?
Answer: It can be towed. There are some considerations. For example, if it’s going on a rollback, you’ll want to be mindful of height on account of low clearances, low hanging tree branches and power lines, etc. Now there may be instances were the tires stick out further than the deck, and if you have permanent fixed side rails on the deck, that’ll be a problem. Towing them with an autoloader, those don’t have extendable wheel grids, so the tires will hang past the crossbar and l arms. I never had a problem doing it, but some company owners don’t like it. Recently, I came across someone on TikTok out of Texas who makes sleeves/extenders for L arms to deal with this sort of thing… even though the wide tires will still hand past the crossbar, you can extend the l arms out far enough that they’ll come out wider than the tires. With a traditional underlift that doesn’t have an autoloader, you have options. You can extend the wheel grids out on those to match the width of the tires then the L arms install on the outside. If it’s something where the weight exceeds the rating of the L arms, provided you have the right size crossbar and you have the sliders and forks, you can use forks to lift it, instead. When I was running that 16 ton and I had to tow duallies and such, this is what I would do. In the case of a lifted pickup, you’ll want to use an integrated boom truck… even using the fork elements with the built in risers, using the under lift on an independent boom truck may not get you enough height if you’re trying to get it and go without chaining up the rear axle. One of the reasons I prefer an integrated boom over an independent boom and underbody wheel lift (HD independent books with the style of underlift a rotator uses are a different animal), because the crossbar will go as high as the boom goes. So, yeah, they’re towable, but it does hinge on the tow outfit being properly equipped to do so.

Question: What are the differences between 6x2 and 6x4 in an 18-wheeler chassis driveline configurations?
Answer: 6x4 = six wheel ends, four of which are powered 6x2 = six wheel ends, two of which are powered Two wheel ends per axle, so each two power wheel ends represents one live axle. Typical 6x4 configuration is that the driveshaft goes into an interaxle differential and from there to the differential pinions for the axles. People often think an IAD works like a transfer case, but this is incorrect. Power is transmitted to both axles at all times, and it functions as an open differential in the unlocked position, while locking it simply forces both outputs to rotate at matching speed. One peculiar 6x4 vehicle I’ve seen was a Boschung Jet Broom - an apparatus used for clearing snow from runways, and built on a Mercedes-Benz Actros chassis. They normally come in 4x4 configuration, with a drop box type transfer case to supply power to the steer axle, but some had an additional tag axle, as well. 6x2, you might see that a couple different ways. You see what looks like a 6x4 tractor, but the forward drive axle has your traditional double treads and the rear axle has a wide base single, that’s what you’re looking at. The wide base singles have less rolling resistance and the difference in tire circumference is irrelevant as that’s a dead axle. That axle may or may not be a lift axle and another giveaway will be the hub itself, where you’ll see an oil or grease cap rather than an axle shaft flange. Here’s one example of a 6x2, with a lifting tag axle on the rear. If you look at the hubs, you can see what I was talking about. Another 6x2 truck, this being one of the Eddie Stobart trucks from the UK. This one uses a pusher axle in front of the live axle, rather than a tag axle behind it. Peculiar layout I’ve seen in photos of trucks from China. This one is a 6x2, but uses two steer axles and a single live axle.

Question: What are the most essential tools and equipment needed to start a roadside assistance business without towing?
Answer: So you're talking about just doing light service, which will consist of tire service (installing spare tires and airing up tires.. I'm not aware of any RSAPs which plug tires, and plugging isn't legal in all states anyhow), jump starts, and lockout service. Those three should be pretty consistent throughout. Fuel deivery may be a possibility, and if you contract with AAA as a full on battery and light service technician, battery installation and testing (although the battery test AAA uses are absolute crap) would be included in that. Of course, the first thing you'll need is a vehicle adequate for the task. I can think of a couple I'd use. Something comparable to the Subaru Outback or Forrester would work nicely. To that end, you don't even really need a wagon... I've seen some of these Agero contractors running around in a two door sedan. If I were doing fuel delivery, I'd probably prefer a small pickup, because I don't want fuel cans in the cabin with me. This is something I'd really like to have one of the older Nissan D21s for. One with the extended cab so I could have tools behind the seat, I'd put a curbside toolbox on it, and have an open air space in the back to keep the fuel can in for fuel deliveries. But I would look for something that met requirements both for usable cargo space and efficiency, unless I was doing batteries. We have a AAA exclusive contractor here with battery technicians... not Pete's, some other one I can't remember the name of... and they're using Ram ProMaster City vans (a badge enginered Nissan NV200) for their battery techs... and for all the weight they carry in batteries, those little 2.5L powered vans suck. Now, I would at least get a magnetic beacon light to put on the roof - and a proper Class II light at that, not the cheapest crap you can find on Amazon. I see some of these dillweeds out here and they have some crappy beacon light from Harbor Freight or Autozone not even adequate to use on a forklift. If you're on the side of the Interstate, you need to make yourself seen. It won't save you - drivers are idiots, but it can at least give the state more leverage to prosecute them after they kill you through their negligence. Strobes are an option as well, but again, get good ones.. Maxxima, Whelen, Grote, etc. It can't hurt to get the Guardian Angel strobes you wear on your person, though in all honesty, I've only seen them used in Tiktok videos by people plugging them - never in person. How you mark your vehicle is up to you. If you're using your daily driver to do this stuff, you may not necessarily wish to put something like DOT C2, SOLAS, or whatever relfective tape on it. You will want signage, and magnetic signs will be find. Swoop/Agero in particular has been cracking down on contractors for not having any signage on their vehicles. And if you sign on as an in-network contractor with AAA, you'll be required to display their logo, as well. PPE... at the very least, ANSI Class II vest, or you can wear shirts and other apparel appropriate for the environment you're working in. The ANSI rated shirts are also vented and breathable, and you can get whatever base color.. the ANSI rating is based on the amount of reflective yellow tape they display, so the rating doesn't change if the base color is orange, pink, blue, black, etc. Because again, if you're on the side of the busy road, you want to make yourself visible. The fashion police can get bent on that one. Gloves.. I really don't like the leather work gloves. They're too inflexible. What are good are the Hardy branded gloves from Harbor Freight that you can get for like five Dollars and change per pair. Buy a few pairs at a time, they even offer them in hi vis yellow (they used to also have orange, but I think those were discontinued) if you should so wish. If you're dealing with batteries, safety glasses. AAA, you're supposed to have them on whenever you open the hood of a member vehicle. I never did, but if the regional motor club has their own towing and recovery company in the area, their supervisors will be running around to spot check both their employees and independent contractors on calls. Flashlights are a must. Personally, I like the Streamlight Wedge, but they're a bit pricey. I bought a less expensive one from Autozone which was pretty decent... the only markings on it said "Police Security". It was right by the counter. I think ~$20 or so. Headlamps are good, as well. One I got from Cornwell was branded BlueIon (P/N CBI4020) and I use it in the shop. It's an excellent light, though the lifespan especially on the high setting isn't the best. Fortunately, it recharges with a USB-C cable. I believe the exact same one is sold at Lowe's Home Improvement under the Kobalt brand, as well. You will of course need a smartphone and/or tablet, as all of this stuff is app based now. And you'll want to install a good stand for whatever you're using or have a good holder for it. I actually found some good non-permanent mounts on Temu... one attaches to the rearview mirror and is good for a phone, another goes into your cupholder, adjusts to fit, is weighted, and can accommodate a phone and even some tablets (my iPad Mini 5 can fit on it). And of course a charger. And speaking of, if you don't have adequate outlets to charge the stuff you have, you may consider installing something like a USB block, additional round 12V ports, etc. If you do fuel delivery, you'll of course need vented gas cans. IIRC, the standard amount delivered by most (if not all) RSAPs is two gallons. If you want to carry a diesel can as well, that's up to you. If I'm pressed for space with everything else, I wouldn't bother, but if I had plenty of space, then I would. And some funnels of varying types, of course. For tire services, do not count on the member/customer having the equipment which originally came with their vehicle. Roll your own. You'll want a floor jack. Me, I'd go for the Daytona 3 ton low profile Rapid Pump floor jack from Harbor Freight (the one Snap-On sued Harbor Freight over), which I think the part number is something like FJ3000 or something like that. But the smaller 1.5 ton floor jack (which is a pretty generic design, and I believe the exact same one is sold by Harbor Freight under the Pittsburgh name, Autozone under the Duralast name, etc.) may be a better choice, because if you have to park outside and go into a parking structure to get to a customer vehicle, that'll travel a lot easier than the big 3 ton Daytona. Also, get a good solid length of 4x4 and 2x4 and cut them into maybe 6" pieces... you try using those little 1.5 ton jacks on something like a full size pickup (and often on vehicles smaller than that), you'll find that they don't have enough reach when you use the factory lift points on the vehicle and will have to use to use the wood blocks to get your necessary height or you may have to set the wheel end back down with the rim off of it, and I'd much rather set a caliper down on a piece of wood than on the ground. You may also find yourself in situations where the ground under the car is soft and causes your jack to sink, then you use the wood underneath it to give it a bigger footprint and distribute the pressure over a larger surface area. Then of course tools to remove and install the wheels. If you just want to use a four way, shake your groove thing. Me, I prefer to use sockets. I carried two sets of flip sockets... one from Cornwell (most likely a rebranded Lisle or Lang product) and another from Mac (which might be indigenous to them or a rebrand). The nice thing about the Mac set is that it had those stupid ".5" metric sizes some Ford, GM, and Stellantis products use. I also carried a set of metric and SAE 1/2" drive sockets (impact sockets in this case). But you may also want to carry some chrome ones, in the off chance that you encounter aftermarket rims where the cavity around the lug nugs is too tight for the thick walls of impact sockets. There are some foldable four ways which work for that, though. If you want to carry an impact wrench, that's up to you. Just don't be one of these dickheads who uses it to install the lug nuts and just hammers and hammers on it. That's how you bugger and stretch the lugs. For what you'd be dealing with, the torque for the lug nuts would generally range from 90 ft/lbs. (small cars and trucks) to ~150 ft/lbs (3/4 and one ton vans and pickups). Me, I carried a torque wrench and if I wanted to use the impact wrench to put them on, I'd only do enough to snug them then use a torque wrench. Otherwise, it was all by hand with a ratchet. You may be required to carry jack stands as well. I'll tell you right now, I'm very much guilty of not using them on roadside calls, but if they're required equipment, then they're required. You'll want something to inflate tires with. When I had a truck which didn't have either an air brake system or an installed air compressor, I went to Amazon and bought a tire inflator.... I ended up getting one from Astro AI, which is nice in that it can use a 20V Li-Ion battery, 12 VDC, or 120 VAC. The downside is that a 2 aH battery is all they offered. I saw at Walmart they had one from Hart, and the 5 aH Hart batteries were only something like $79. Incidentally, Hart also has impact wrenches, so you could use one battery for multiple tools. Lockouts... most RSAPs don't want you using anyting beyond a basic prying wedge, air wedge, long reach, and sully strip and/or remote button. And if you don't know what you're doing with them, you really have no business using lockout tools which go into the door cavity... you can easily tear into a wiring harness, especially with current model cars. For the long reach, I recommend the single piece ones over the sectioned ones... yeah, they don't store as easily, but the connection points on the sectioned ones aren't malleable. For the prying wedge, the black plastic ones with a straight wedge at one end and which are curved at the other and have a rubber bumper at the bottom have kind become standard (High Tech and Access Tools are among those marketing something like that), but sometimes they're too thick for what you are trying to get into, and you'll find the little white basic wedges from the Steck "Big Easy" kits work much better. Anyhow, make sure you know what the hell you're doing before you start offering lockout service. See if the local pull and pay yards will let you in just to practice doing lockouts... two of the people living with me work for the regional affiliate motor club doing roadside assistance, and that's what I did with them... took them to LKQ, sweet talked them into letting us in without charging us, and we went around to various vehicles and practiced doing lockouts with them. Jump starts, of course you'll need a booster pack. And in the spirit of not being a dillweed, don't get these tiny little boosters like those dinky little Type S ones they sell at Costco for $60 thinking that'll have what it takes to jump start the pickup with the 6.7 diesel. My brand of choice was always Noco... at a minimum, I'd recommend the GB70, better still is the GB150, even better yet (but more costly) is the GBX-155. I would carry that AND one of the older style lead acid boosters because you might run into that guy who uses his AAA Plus RV membership to jump start an RV built from an old commuter bus that was powered by an 8V92T Detroit. And on that note, know the fuck what you're looking at when you observe a vehicle charging system if you're gonna deal with these RVs. Some of these buses have a 24V cranking system and you do not want to connect jumper cables connected to a 12V vehicle or a 12V booster across that. Better you should mark that call as incomplete and let them get a proper heavy duty service out there... thing of it is, most RSAPs don't have HD service providers in their network, so they have to go out of network for it... when that happens, they pay full price and so they try to avoid doing that, and you end up in situations where you have someone with no automotive background prior and in their first roadside assistance job struggling to figure out why they can't jump start the RV built on a bus chassis with a 24V cranking system. But I'm kinda airing my grievances with RSAPs (especially AAA) at this point. On the subject of AAA, if you're an in-network provider, they'll expect you to perform their halfassed battery tests when you do a jump start. Even as a tow technician working for a motor club tow company, I always just noted them as "inconclusive results" because I knew their tests were absolute crap. Then you decide who you'll want to be in-network and out of network for. Honk, I will not accept any of their calls. Aside from their low rates, they have a propensity to claim that completed calls were canceled and refusing payment. The tow company I'm invested in, we completely block them on Towbook. Swoop/Agero rates are still kinda... meh. NSD (Nation Safe Drivers)/Quest is a mixed bag... sometimes their rates are better, sometimes they're not really any better than Honk, but they don't shaft you out of payment. Allied and Allstate offer better rates. If you're doing Allstate calls on a weekend, you won't be able to amend those calls, but that's more applicable to the tow side (e.g., you end up needing to use dollies on a tow call which didn't originally call for them). AAA is one I stay out of network with. I haven't had any dealings with Good Sam's at all, and I couldn't even tell you if they actually are their own motor club or if they simply run through one of the ones I've mentioned already. If you have follow up questions, you're free to message me.

Question: What features and specifications are most important to you when selecting a truck for your business, and how can a Mack Truck meet those needs to enhance your operations?
Answer: Dump trucks are all we have from Mack anymore. We sold off the heavy haul units with the MP10s since they stopped marketing and seemingly supporting that engine here. Camelback suspension is good for a vocational truck, though I really don’t feel like it’s intrinsically better than a walking beam or Chalmers. Air ride for highway trucks is pretty run-of-the-mill. Mack MDrive is a Volvo IShift. If you’re getting an AMT with the “Mack” engine, that’s what you end up with, else you get an Eaton with a Cummins… I don’t believe Mack offers the Allison TC10, but I could be mistaken. Manuals, the triple counter shaft Mack transmissions are much sturdier than the Eaton twin counter shaft manuals. The trade off being they’re a little more difficult (especially if you’re accustomed to the Eatons), and higher maintenance. If we were talking a truck that was operating in the woods, by all means the Mack transmissions. If we’re talking a highway truck, I’d opt for the Eaton or an AMT. Mack rears are what I’d want for an off highway application, but not for a highway application. Not to mention Mack won’t spec out a truck higher than ~430 hp with the 93 series and make you get either the 200 series or vendor axles. The 93s are heavy already, but the 200s, those are seriously heavy. Engines are Volvo engines with a different paint color and name on the valve cover. Support leaves a bit to be desired. If I were in the market, for me to specifically seek out a Mack truck, it would have to be because I wanted the Mack axles. Otherwise I can’t see how my needs wouldn’t be better met by Freightliner or Kenworth, especially from the dealer support angle.

Question: What if the US military adopted the AR-10 over the T48 (FN FAL) and T44 (Grand with a few extra steps) prototypes as the M14?
Answer: This is actually an interesting question. If they had the prototypes available in time with regular steel barrels and ended up getting the contract to replace the Garand, a lot could have changed. The AR-15 was originally intended to replace the M1 and M2 carbines. Experience with the AR-10 would have probably left the Army advised ahead of time that the -15s would require cleaning kits, thus avoiding some of the problems they had initially, but it might also slow down the improvements which resulted in the M16A1. Armalite probably wouldn’t have sold the design to Colt and would’ve continued working on that, and the AR-18 never would’ve been, meaning a lot of designs which used that action later on would probably end up quite different. I think the difference would’ve been decided depending on whether they continued using the AR-10 in Vietnam or decided to use the AR-15 (which would’ve been seen as a carbine, and thus the M16 would’ve ended up having the M4 nomenclature). If it had been used as a weapon for support units, the effectiveness of the 5.56 round and results of Project SALVO may not have been fully assessed, and the US may have ended up developing a new round closer in dimension to the M1943 round used by the Kalashnikov rather than standardizing on the 5.56. Which means the AK-74 may have never been, as that round was developed based on observations of the 5.56 being used in Vietnam. Which means the full potential of the 5.56 may have never been realized, but we might have ended up with a round which did better at retaining muzzle energy at range, and that would’ve been helpful when the Taliban would set up 500 meters or so out once they figured out the shortcomings of the 5.56 at those ranges. The .50 I was on had no problem reaching out and touching them nor did our M240s, but the most common weapons used against them of course were the individual weapons, which were the M4 and M16A4 when I was there. On the flip side, I ended up with a few dents in my chicken plate. Or maybe we’d end up at the same place. It really would depend on whether or not the adoption of the AR-10 led to the Air Force not purchasing AR-15s and whether or not troops deploying to Vietnam continued using the AR-10s or were issued M16s instead.

Question: What is the hardest instrument to find for a band?
Answer: I’m not normally one to disagree with Rik Elswit on matters of music, but I think it really depends on what the band’s niche is and how uncommon a certain instrument is within that niche. I know some people who formed a punk band. The frontman’s girlfriend happened to play the harp. It became a very prominent part of their music. They broke up, she left the band. How do you think their search for another harp player is going? Aside from those not being people you happen across every day, of the handful you might meet, how many of them are really interested in that sort of band? Which, I thought using the harp was really cool (or even that she had a harp to begin with), though the music is much too ‘poppy’ for my liking. Among the various instruments I play, the second one I learned was the flute (and I springboarded into other woodwind instruments from there). While a rarity in genres such as punk and metal, it’s not entirely unheard of. Somewhere out there is probably a metal band who wants to incorporate a flutist into their music. They’ve probably spoken to several people who play the flute, but do not give two shits about that type of music. And here I am, but our paths are never going to cross. You can find someone to play any instrument as a guest musician. On my first solo product album, the outtro track included a didgeridoo track recorded for me by someone from Boulder, Colorado. He could make a guest appearance, but he would never be interested in being a permanent member of such a band. Vocalists, I think really depends on how flexible the style of music you play is. My background is primarily in punk and metal, and of the latter you can see a spread which ranges from operatic voices (e.g., Tarja Turunen, Liv-Kristine Espenæs, Veronika Sevostyanova, etc.) to people who might be good vocalists but crap singers, yet it works for what they’re playing (e.g., Mike Williams, King Foley), and anything in-between and beyond. Now finding a vocalist with a specific sound whose vision of music coincides with yours is a bit more of a challenge, but all in all, I think the answer to this question is going to be a variable.

Question: What weapon from today, if given to a WW2 soldier, would be most useful/popular, if ammunition and parts were available?
Answer: I wouldn’t make a huge technological jump. You provide ammunition and parts, with no mention of logistics or technical know how. Look at car repair questions on Quora, people can very easily get parts, but still have no clue what to do to get their cars running properly again. You just drop a bunch of… whatever… Javelin missiles, Apache helicopters, F35s, etc. in the middle of WWII, you’ve got that same problem. They’re not just going to pick it up and know what to do, how to maintain it, etc. There’s also the logistics matter. You have the ammo, cool. Now there’s the whole supply chain and getting it to where it needs to be. Why did the Warsaw Pact and NATO standardize their ammunition? Logistics. Then of course technical knowledge. I’m typing this out on a device which fits in the palm of my hand yet has more computing power than ENIAC, which filled a whole room. ENIAC was more than most people in the 1940s could comprehend, let alone a smart phone. So unless you’re providing that yourself, you need to train people, and for such a technological leap, it’s going to take much longer for people who’ve never seen an electronic computer before than it will for people who grew up with them. Parts don’t mean shit if you can’t figure out when they’re needed, nor if a system goes down for reasons that won’t be fixed by simply throwing parts at it. So I wouldn’t leap too far. FN-49, 7.92x57 This would be with the UK in mind, as they had tested prototypes of it before the war and has that round in their inventory, not to mention they certainly captured plenty of it as well. Uzi, Mini-Uzi, Micro Uzi, 9x19 Developed in 1949, so it’s well within the technical capabilities of the 1940s. I would have this in mind more for partisans in France, Yugoslavia, Norway, etc. AKM, 7.62x39 Of course with the Soviet Union in mind. They were already producing the cartridge for the SKS and RPD machine guns in the later years of WWII, and the original AK-47 would appear shortly after the war. Using sheet metal stamping rather than milling and other improvements, they would’ve benefited greatly from it. PSL, 7.62x54R Another one with the Soviet Union in mind, especially given the amount of urban fighting they were doing. I chose the Romanian PSL rather than the Soviet PSD because this uses the same action as the AK and would allow concurrent training on both this and the AK. M79 grenade launcher I remember reading about the Japanese leg mortars and how effectively they could be used, while the Allies had nothing comparable. These could certainly help close that gap and increase a platoon’s overall firepower. Carl Gustaf Introduced in 1948 and still in use. I think that alone says plenty. Alvis Saladin/Saracen/et. al. This would be a vast improvement over the M8 Greyhound, and this family of vehicles could potentially introduce new doctrines which would lead to more effective troop movements. It’s not a huge technological leap, and in the case of the Saladin, it could smoke any armored car it encountered without braking a sweat and probably a good number of tanks in service, as well, especially in the earlier years of the war. Sikorsky H-19 and H-34 H-21 Bump the timeline ahead and introduce helicopters into the fold. These should all be within the technical capability range of the 1940s. Logistics, medevac, etc. They would’ve been a huge benefit. The French also introduced the use of them as gunships, arming their H-21s in Algeria. C119 C123 More capable cargo aircraft? Yes, please. B36 Peacemaker Getting close enough to bomb Japan wouldn’t have been a question. English Electric Canberra Every bit as fast as the Me.262, capable of carrying as much as a B-17 could internally for short range missions but with more range, this would’ve made a huge difference. And of course Korean War era jet fighters were probably within the realm of feasibility for people in the 1940s, like the P80, F86, MiG-15, Hawker Hunter, etc. Maybe I’m right, maybe I’m wrong, but those are the things I’d go with.

Question: What are air fittings used for in trucks?

You may find those types of fittings, you may find push-in fittings… … you may find compression fittings which crush a ferrel against the hose to keep the connection secure (not sure if this truck has any or not). Quiz time, kids… what’s specific about DOT brass and why is it so? If you mean an air coupler like those used for air tools… … (or conversely, you may see a valve core and stem like those used to inflate tires) that allows you to supply surrogate air (such as shop air, air from another truck, etc.) to the system and they’ll be used in conjunction with a ball valve or a one way check valve. For example, we do our own towing and recovery in-house. So if a tractor-trailer’s compressor craps out, and the complete unit has to be towed (or even just to separate the power unit from the trailer so another truck can take it), I can connect a hose from the emergency line glad hand if the wrecker to supply the pneumatic system of the casualty truck and just release the brakes with the MV3 valve rather than having to cage all the brake chambers and uncage them later on.

Question: Is a rear cargo box really that dangerous? Does it really make the car more unstable?
Answer: It can be, yes. If you overload it. Whenever you have anything that’s hitched to the back of your car or overhanging from it, think of your rear axle as a fulcrum at that point. Take too much weight off your steer axle, and it’ll cause you problems with steering, traction (especially in the case of FWD cars), and braking (since most vehicles up to 1/2 ton pickups still primarily use the brakes on the steer axle). So if you get a cargo box and say you put 200 lbs. in it and you put it on the back of a Suburban, you’re looking at a curb weight of 5,600 - 6,000 lbs., with the majority of that being on the steer axle, with a wheelbase of 134”. The Suburban will shrug that off. Do that to a Sonic on the other hand, with half the curb weight of less and 34” less of wheelbase, and you’ll be having problems.

The administration in office - that being, the Biden administration - got the blame. He’ll have something to say, alright, but it won’t be under after the fact, when he’s faced with the realization that his illegal immigrants weren’t given any special exemption. Question: If an officer calls a tow truck to move a driver, who's also present but out of gas, does this mean the car will be impounded too?
Answer: A rotation call. That sucks for you, because rotations are billed at the prevailing rate. And if that call is at the behest of the department and in his official capacity as an LEO, it is a rotation call. If you can get your vehicle out of the way and even if you have to do a cash call for fuel delivery from a tow company, it’ll cost less than the rotation. But if you’re blocking a roadway and immobilized, they don’t call for fuel delivery - they call to have the car towed and it is a rotation call. Now in some states they do have a sponsored roadside assistance service, typically in conjunction with local companies through an insurance company as proxy. Those will deliver fuel. In Denver, I’ve seen trucks with Allstate markings on them doing this. Here in Raleigh, it’s sponsored by Geico, and they have pickups with arrow boards in the back. But I only see them on freeways… if your issue occurs on a two lane backroad in the county without enough of a shoulder to get your car safely clear of the lane of travel, it’s going to be a rotation call unless you’ve already called for roadside and your cavalry arrives before theirs does. If you’re not being arrested, they can be converted to a cash call. I’ve had it before where someone didn’t want their car impounded, converted to a cash call, and we stopped at an ATM on the way to the address of their choosing. Now if you can’t do this, then it goes into impound. For accidents where you’re certain the car will be totaled, it’s beneficial to the owner and there is no up front cost to them… the insurance company or whoever buys the car from the insurance company (e.g., Copart) takes care of that.

Question: What exactly is a US Military drivers license?
Answer: Military vehicles fall into an exempted class as far as civilian licensing goes. To drive this in a nonexempt capacity as a civilian requires a Commercial Drivers License, which is federally administered but issued by the operator’s state of residence. To operate this as a military service member in the course of your duties does not require a Commercial Drivers License. As far as your civilian license goes, there is no upgrade required (although I have heard of states which have members of their National Guard require license upgrades other than a CDL for when those vehicles are used in service of the state). Now a civilian contractor, vendor, etc. who happens to be operating one of these doesn’t fall under that exemption and would require the CDL. Well, the military isn’t just going to hand you the keys (they don’t use a key switch for the ignition, but they still run cables through the steering wheel and secure it with a padlock to keep some random jackass from just driving off with it) and say, “Have at it”. They’re going to put you through training and determine when you’re qualified to operate it. To show this qualification, you get a laminated slip of paper with all the vehicles you’ve qualified according to the military to operate. In the Army, this form was called a DA348. This is a sample I found online. I won’t post mine because some of the information on it falls under PII which should be kept secure. The DA348 is a long form and then we got a short form to carry with us as our license to display when we had to. By the book, you’re supposed to test and be licensed on every single submodel and variant you operate. In practice, this wasn’t done so strictly. Take, for example, the M923 5 ton cargo truck. Question: What was it like growing up in a Mennonite community?
Answer: Restricted. I went to secular schools, so I had exposure to the ‘English’, but this was in the part of Wisconsin you could only tell wasn’t Alabama in a picture by the snow, and a trip to the “big city” meant Sheboygan. Of course, everyone had Internet access. But of course I didn’t, though a friend did give me her old iPod, which I made sure I kept hidden from my parents. The farmer next door was ‘English’, and sometimes their family would watch my sister and I when my parents had their own date nights. He was a ham radio operator, and I think I was 10 when he let me key up under his call sign on I think a 20 meter radio, and I got a reply! From Belgium! For those of you who’ve always had ready access to this connectivity, being able to Skype, FaceTime, etc. at will with people the world over, I don’t know if you can really understand how drastic this was for me. I’d lived in a box in rural Wisconsin. On occasion, we visited relatives in Ontario, Indiana, and Ohio. Anything else sounded like some fantasy land. I knew of other countries and was pretty decent at geography, but that was the first time any of them had actually been on any sort of reach. And then a couple weeks later my neighbor received a QR card from him, which he gave to me, and I still have it, so when people look at me funny and ask why someone like me would get into something like ham radio as a hobby, that’s the reason. That’s where my wanderlust began. Of course, plenty of hypocrisy and sewn mouth secrets in that community. I think I brought my parents a lot of grief, because I wouldn’t think twice to question and even challenge community elders, which was a big no-no, especially as a possessor of lady bits. Shunning, people generally seem to know it’s a thing. I never baptized into the church, so I couldn’t be shunned. I’d still talk to people who were, which there was no prohibition on it since I wasn’t a member of the church, but the elders and Dudley Do-Rights didn’t like it. I suppose they could’ve threatened my parents with shunning if they didn’t reel me in, but they were too dependent on my family to jeopardize that over me. So I got away with quite a bit. And they think my leaving was the end of that, but my parents have a surprise in store for them. If you think ‘English’ girls like to gossip, we one upped them. The only difference was that it stayed among us, and didn’t spread outside of that. I swear, you even talked to one of the boys in the community, right away, it was, “So are you going to marry him?”. One boy in particular, they thought for sure we would marry. They didn’t understand I only tolerated him. At some point he got that idea in his head. Really pissed me off because when I insisted on continuing with high school (8th grade was typically the point when children of the Anabaptist faiths were pulled out of school), he kept trying to dissuade me from it because I had “womanly duties to tend to” and such. Meanwhile, the girl who actually did have a thing for him got pissed off at me, even though I had absolutely zero interest in the guy, and I never claimed otherwise. They did end up marrying, and she in particular was not happy to see me when I went back to visit a few years back along with my sister and an Amish runaway whose path ended up crossing with mine. Probably made worse by… I hate to say it, but she puffed out like a popcorn kernel. As for the rest, ours wasn’t a horse and buggy sect. I grew up on a working farm, we had machinery (and I picked up a peculiar interest in it, leading to where I am now). Gender roles are very cast, but a lack of available people to hire plus an aptitude for certain tasks on my end led to me having to fulfill roles outside of the gender norms. But I was raised to be the perfect little subservient housewife. Suffice to say, that’s not how it played out. As for the ‘English’, we did get picked on quite a bit, but there also those who’d step in to tell them to leave us alone. Nonresistance and nonviolence were a big part of the upbringing and they knew it. I think one of the big pivotal moments for me was during high school, one of the boys had been harassing me constantly. One day he cornered, told me I was going to give him a blowjob, and actually went and pulled his dick out. Something in me snapped that day, and I ended up grabbing a pencil and stabbing him in his dick. Other kids at the school, their parents, and even the parents of the boy who got the surprise Prince Albert supported me… my community scorned me. We were supposed to practice no resistance, violence is never the answer… except I couldn’t help but feel like it was in that instance. I had doubts about the Mennonite life being for me. That’s the point where I knew for sure that it wasn’t. But at the same time, once I started living a ‘worldly’ life, there were facets of the previous life which hadn’t made sense to me before but suddenly did. I think my parents hoped I’d come back to it, baptize, be the ideal little housewife I was expected to be. Hopefully they figured out by now that’s not happening.

Question: What is the function of a tractor protection valve?
Answer: Opens and closes the air supply to the trailer. You’ll have two lines coming out of it… emergency and supply. There’s a plunger inside the TPV which is pushed down by signal air when the brake control valve (PP-7 or PP-7 side of an MV-3 valve) is depressed. The input to the emergency line is plumbed directly to the primary air system reservoir and will always be charged with air when the plunger is depressed. The service port will have two inputs, with one coming off the pedal/treadle valve (the valve actuated by the brake pedal) and the other - if equipped - to the trolley valve which actuates just the trailer brakes (if the truck isn’t so equipped, the input will simply be capped off).

Question: What is the function of a relay valve in an air braking system?
Answer: Uses a small current to move a larger current. They’re used for the service brake chambers on the drive axle(s) and some use them on the steer axle as well. Signal air is sent through the foot valve (pedal valve or treadle valve). When it gets to the relay valve, it pushes down a plunger. This opens the ports inside the valve and also blocks the exhaust port. The inlet port will be plumbed directly to a reservoir - primary air system for the primary axle of a truck; secondary air system for the steer axle and any tag or pusher axles on the vehicle). When the plunger is pushed down, it opens up a path from that inlet port to the discharge port, and that air will flow across and fill up the service diaphragms in the brake chambers. When the signal air is cut off, a spring pushes the plunger back up and air is evacuated from the brake chamber diaphragms through the exhaust port.

Question: What is the function of the unloader valve in an air braking system?
Answer: When the reservoirs reach cut out pressure, the unloading valve is depressed in the air compressor. This shuts off the outlet to the discharge air and puts the air in the compressor in a recirculating state. This is inportant, because this is when the air compressor cools down. When cut in pressure is reached, the air governor closes, air is no longer supplied to push down the unloading valve, and a spring pushes it back up, at which point the compressor goes back into a loaded state and discharges air to the reservoirs again.

Question: The engine in the Tesla cybertruck is rated at 850 HP and 12000 ft lbs of torque about 6x more then semi truck or heavy equipment engines. Why haven't equipment manufacturers put these vastly more powerful engines in their products?
Answer: The actual engine torque is about 860 ft./lbs. for the 2024 Tesla Cybertruck as a single motor, RWD and about 1,030 ft./lbs. for the tri motor “Cyberbeast”. A typical Class 8 truck tractor engine in the US will produce 1,400 - 1,800 ft. lbs. and anywhere from 400 - 600 horsepower. You gave an exaggerated number - it’s actually 10,296 ft./lbs. and 845 hp for the Cyberbeast. Which are impressive numbers, but that’s a measure of wheel torque, achieved through reduction gearing, not what’s going into the planetary gearset. If you tried running 10k of torque directly through a pair of 20k axles pulling a load, you’d destroy them. So the engine has considerably more horsepower, this much is true, but considerably less torque, and that’s what matters. However, when it comes to wheel torque, you actually are right about that. However, part of what produces that number is the tire circumference, and the Cybertruck running LT265/R20 at 583 revolutions per mile (~363 revolutions per kilometer) isn’t going to produce the same numbers as a Class 8 running, say, 11R24.5s at 475 revolutions per mile isn’t going to show the same numbers. If you were to electrify the existing driveline of a Class 8 and put a motor generator directly to the interaxle differential, you would substantially reduce driveline loss. The viability of an electric Class 8 has already been proven… to an extent. Now find charging stations in the middle of Montana, Central Texas, or the Dakotas. Not to mention the trucks are heavy, with the Tesla truck tractor being the worst offender at 26 - 27k, whereas your typical 6x4 sleeper berth truck weighs in around 18 - 20k. With bridge law formula capping the interstate statutory weight at 80k for a five axle unit, moving the same amount of product is going to require more trucks and drivers in an industry already constantly declaring itself hindered by driver shortages. So, why don’t we don’t uproot the entire industry overnight and push electric truck tractors in spite of a lack of logistical support for them and which results in an increased demand for bodies in seats when the industry professes to be struggling to meet numbers as is? Go ahead and put two and two together. What’s another common industry complaint? Not enough truck parking. Then you factor in range. Tesla has talked about 300 and 500 mile ranges for their trucks, and that’s most likely under nominal conditions. Take a flatbed or lowboy or any type of open deck trailer with a load that doesn’t have particularly ideal aerodynamics, and that range will decrease. Take a truck running through the Rockies all day vs. one running through the Arizona desert and you’ll see significant differences. That only accounts for the driving portion. OTR drivers tend to pretty much live in their trucks for their duration on the road. Of course they don’t want to freeze in the Winter or roast in the Summer, which means power will be used to run the climate control. Tl:dr, the numbers don’t reflect exactly what you think they do, the industry isn’t ready for that change, nor will it be an instantaneous thing, and it’s still a maturing technology which isn’t quite prepared for that particular task, though of course it certainly has viability in certain facets of the industry as it currently stands.

Question: Is a deuce and a half a commercial vehicle if I wanted to register it as such and pull a trailer? The tandem axles, air over hydraulic brakes and the size and weight should make it a commercial vehicle?
Answer: GVWR for an M35 series is around 22,000, which puts it below CDL weight, but above the 10,000 GVWR threshold which would require it to have an FHWA annual inspection, permits, etc. and for the operator to have a DOT medical card in interstate operation and have one for intrastate operation of their state requires it. The tandem axles don’t make a difference except when it comes to exempt use in California, but that’s its own can of worms. Looking at the other answers, you’ve been getting some bad information here. The FMCSA threshold for defining a Commercial Motor Vehicle insofar as weight goes is 10,000 lbs. (when used in interstate commerce), not the 26,000 lb. threshold required for a CDL. Yes, you would have to make some modifications to the vehicle (for one, you’d have to add an electric windshield defroster, rework the brake lights, etc.), but yes, you could get it registered as a CMV, but this would also have to be done before you road tested in it - they won’t let you do your CDL skills test and road test in an exempted vehicle, even a Category A vehicle. Because weight rating alone doesn’t make it a commercial vehicle, else every Cletus Bob with an F350 would have to get commercial plates, insurance, annual FHWA, etc. for theirs. Though I really shouldn’t be talking shit there, as I also own a one ton pickup, albeit one I inherited rather than bought. Air over hydraulic brakes… irrelevant. So, what type of brake system the vehicle uses has absolutely zero determination as to whether it requires a CDL or not. The criteria for it requiring a CDL are that it’s used in a non-exempt capacity and one or more of the following: Says nothing about the presence or absence of air brakes, and you will not find any stipulation that a vehicle requires a CDL on account of air brakes from the FMCSA or any state DOT. Now it does get weird regarding air brakes. If you don’t complete and pass the written air brakes test and complete and pass the skills test in a vehicle equipped with a full air brake system, you get a restriction prohibiting you from operating any vehicle requiring a CDL which is equipped with air brakes. Air over hydraulic is not a full air brake system, and you would likewise have that restriction. Where it gets screwy is that someone could use an F350 and a gooseneck trailer to get a Class A CDL, and let’s say they get a hazmat endorsement. With that being a hydraulic brake power unit and electric brake trailer, they’ll get the air brake restriction. But let’s say they get a job driving a box truck; and it’s a 26,000 GVWR Ford F650 with air brakes. They could drive it, as you wouldn’t need a CDL to operate it. But if it carried a quantity of hazardous material which required placards to be displayed, he wouldn’t be able to legally drive it because of the restriction, but could drive a hydraulic brake equipped F650 with that same hazmat load. But let’s say later on he becomes a direct (W2/W4) employee of a farmer, they’re in a state which applies the farm truck exemption to Category A combinations (the FMCSA does, but not all states do), and the farmer has a tractor-trailer with a full air brake system plated as a farm truck and used within the criteria and limitations of exempt farm use, our same guy could legally drive that without issue. Sounds like a hot mess, doesn’t it? So, let’s say you decide you want to use that old M35 for a business. You got your USDOT or state exemption number for your business, you got your fuel tax sticker, your FHWA annual inspection, you’ve got it plated with a plate applicable to a commercial operation, now you want to use it to get your CDL. To get a Class C CDL, which is for Category C vehicles (those with a GVWR of less than 26,000 lbs.) because you need one of the endorsements only available with a CDL for the way you’re going to be using the truck, yes, you could use it for your skills test. You would get either a “L” or “Z” restriction which prohibited you from operating a vehicle requiring a CDL which has a full air brake system. If the truck in question was an M35A3, which used an Allison HT series automatic transmission rather than a manual transmission, you would also get an “E” restriction which prohibited you from operating any CDL vehicle equipped with a manual transmission (as with the air brake restriction, it would not apply to non-CDL - including exempted - vehicles). Class B CDL, not gonna happen. The GVWR of those is ~22,000 lbs. and so the state would plate it as a 26k truck. Not heavy enough to qualify as a Category B vehicle. Class A CDL, if you put a trailer with a GVWR of more than 10,000 lbs. behind it, yes. Let’s say your business ventures have you towing a skid loader behind it and so you use a 16,000 GVWR trailer to do that with. Between that truck and that trailer, you have a Category A combination and your using it in a revenue generating operation means it doesn’t qualify for exempted use. Yes, you could get a Class A that way. You would again have the same restrictions listed above, and if you used any connection other than a fifth wheel for the trailer (such as the pintle and clevice it came with), you would also get an “O” restriction prohibiting you from operating any CDL vehicle with a trailer connected to by a fifth wheel. I know people like for answers on Quora to be simple and fairly short, but this is one of those questions where being short and being concise are anathema to each other.

Question: Do military vehicles have air over hydraulic brakes?
Answer: Some did. The M35 and M39/809 series five tons did. They kinda went the way of the dinosaur and have way to full air brake systems, and on the commercial side gave way to a combination of full air brake systems and hydroboosted hydraulic brakes. It’s a pretty interesting topic, or at least it is to me because I’m a dork like that, but the military was the reason air over hydraulic was developed. During WWII, it offered some very distinct advantages. For one, you didn’t have to wait for the system to air up. Air brake systems of the time, you could roll out without air - they didn’t have spring brakes and the spring brake chamber wasn’t invented until 1957 - but they wouldn’t be able to stop. Whereas with air over hydraulic, you might have to really stand on the brake pedal as you’d have no assist without air, but you could brake. It allows you to couple an air brake trailer to a hydraulic brake truck. Well, you could couple them regardless, it actually use the trailer brakes. Even now, for military trailers with brakes, air is the default, so those water bowsers you see towed behind LMTVs, they’re equipped with air brakes. And before the LMTV came the M35 series, which used air over hydraulic brakes. On the commercial side… the M149 water bowser has an empty weight of around 2,900 lbs. and then it’s rated for 400 gallons of water, so at eight pounds per gallon, that would be another 3,200 lbs., so about 6,100 lbs. all told. A commercial trailer of that weight in the US will use electric brakes (which can be electric friction or electric over hydraulic) or surge brakes. So it’s not really relevant in the commercial side, and that’s one of the reasons air over hydraulic went the way of the dinosaur commercially. It was also more effective using air to boost the braking than vacuum assist was for vehicles that size. Hydroboost - which uses hydraulic pressure from the power steering system to provide brake boost - was a child of the 1970s, and while power steering was invented in 1926, the first commercially available vehicle with it didn’t come about until 1951, and it was only during WWII that an interest in putting it in military vehicles came about, but the vast majority of military vehicles did not have it.

Answer: Prybars from Matco? HA! Their prybars are made by Mayhew, and can be found for considerably less under both the Mayhew and the (Harbor Freight) Icon marques. Matco literally does not manufacture a single tool they sell, though there are some they distribute exclusively (e.g., their ratchets are made for them by AJ Manufacturing, the complete tap and die set they sell is made by Astro, but that specific set is sold only by Matco, etc.), but most of it is rebrands you can get at a better price on Amazon. A good portion of the stuff Mac and Cornwell sells is the same, though each do actually have their own tools, as well. I’m partial to Snap-On’s Dual 80 ratchets, but I don’t need to use theirs. There are people out there doing this job with Pittsburgh ratchets. I like the Snap-On wrenches because their lower profile fits into places others won’t, but if you don’t actually encounter those situations, it won’t make a difference to you. When new techs ask me for advice, mine is to get budget conscious tools which allow them to build up a set more quickly and take on bigger responsibilities, then upgrade as they see fit to. Going from say, a Carlyle wrench to a Snap-On wrench… it’s not like one of those video games where you get a big HP bonus for upgrading to the Mystical Sword of the AIDSmonger or some shit. If there’s a tool brand that’ll actually be essential to you and you’re almost to certain to end up with in your tool assortment, whether under their own name or someone else’s, it’s not Snap-On, Mac, Matco, Cornwell… it’s Lisle. Don’t get me wrong, I have plenty of Snap-On tools and multiple Snap-On toolboxes. But the money I’m making doesn’t reflect someone brand spanking new to the trade either, plus I have other sources of income. You need to be careful with these tool trucks. To be honest, I’m glad we only have two. You get all four and get a truck account with all four of them, say you pay $25/week to Snap-On, the same to Mac, Marco, and Cornwell, you’re looking at $400/month. And many of the dealers want a 10 payment plan, so if you rack up a $500 balance (which is very easy to do), they’ll be wanting $50/week. Then you’ll end up on the corner trying to sell handjobs in order to pay the multiple tool bills you’ve amassed. Now I’m not saying don’t buy Snap-On or Mac or Cornwell tools (I generally try to steer people away from Matco, but I also bought a set of their black ratchets with the purple handles because they look so badass). But do it when you’re ready. I’d be working in the shop for some time before I had to go to a tech program so I met the criteria for a technician job title (which Is amusing to me, as I already had three Master ASE certs plus two Master EVT certs by that time, but I had an equipment operator job title), and these tech school instructors can be some little fucking wannabe pimps. “YoU’lL gEt LaUgHeD oUt Of ThErE iF yOu ShOw Up WiTh CrAfTsMaN tOoLs…”. Quoting the words so eloquently spoken by the late Jim Jones during one of his “White Night” recordings… SHIT! BULLSHIT! Now some things you don’t want to go cheap on. Your basic combination wrenches, for example. I would not use Pittsburgh because those fuckers will break on you. Up to 24mm and 15/16”, splurge a little and get at least the Icon, Milwaukee, or Carlyle wrenches. As much as I do like the stuff made by Apex when it comes to more budget conscious tools, I really don’t like their wrenches and would not get Gearwrench, SATA, Crescent, Husky, or Duralast wrenches. Now once you get above 24mm and 15/16”, you’ve got enough metal you’re not breaking those. I use Sunex jumbo wrenches and Pittsburgh ‘super jumbo” wrenches. Prybars… I wouldn’t go cheap with those either. You can get them from Harbor Freight, but get the Icon ones, not the Pittsburgh ones. As for your ratchets, whatever. At the time the Matco 88 tooth ratchets were designed, they were owned by Apex Tool Group, who also own Gearwrench, Crescent, SATA, and others. That ratchet head on the Matco ratchet is basically the same as the Gearwrench head, and you could even swap internals between the 84 tooth Gearwrench ratchets and 88 tooth Matco ratchets. Likewise, the Husky, Duralast, Crescent, and SATA ratchets are quite similar. I would go for the 72 tooth ones or perhaps the 100 position Husky or Duralast ratchets… the 72 tooth models will work in as tight of a working area as you’re likely to encounter, and the higher the tooth count on the ratchet, the smaller and weaker the teeth are… while the dual pawl mechanisms used in high tooth count ratchets (>90 teeth, although Snappy uses a dual pawl on their 80 tooth ratchets) does offset it somewhat, I’d still avoid these 120, 144, etc. position ratchets. I’m gonna end this here, because this is some shit I can really get carried away on.

Question: What FCC license form do I use for a radio that uses UHF frequencies (currently own a MB400 Midland) can they be used by anyone or only for businesses?
Answer: I’m not terribly familiar with Midland’s business radios, but it’s curious to me they give a list of specific available frequencies rather than a range. For example, if you had a comparable radio from Kenwood, you’d have either a 403 - 430 MHz or 430 - 470 MHz range. Among the available frequencies listed are 464.500 (Brown Dot) and464.550 (Yellow Dot). These are itinerant frequencies, intended to be used for non-stationary purposes. While these frequencies can be used in half duplex operation and run through a repeater, the corresponding repeater inputs - 469.500 (Brown Duplex) and 469.550 (Yellow Duplex) - aren’t listed, which makes me think this radio is not repeater capable (I’ll read through the manual later and edit this if I’m incorrect). You are limited to five watts on these, so you don’t need to go out and get a 100% duty cycle capable repeater and duplexer (which is a moot point anyhow, if your radio isn’t repeater capable to begin with. I have a repeater I made for these frequencies using a camera tripod, a metal ring I welded around it, an extendable handle for painters, tent stakes and rope, a power supply and repeater controller, and two old Kenwood TK-350N handhelds (the “N” indicating that they transmit in narrow band). To be licensed on these frequencies, you need to get licensed for the itinerant frequencies, which you can select statewide itinerant or nationwide itinerant. A lot of people believe these are license by rule frequencies not requiring a license, and that is just incorrect. Now you can’t get any sort of exclusivity on these frequencies… Silver Star (467.850), Gold Star (467.875), Red Star (467.900), and Blue Star (467.925) are also listed frequencies available. These can be used for fixed base operations, and are low power frequencies which can be allocated to several users in a smaller area by the FCC Regional Coordinator than the higher power frequencies. These are also frequencies people mistakenly assume to be license by rule (along with a number of VHF frequencies slotted to the business band). The rest of the available frequencies are from the Business/Industrial pool in the 462 - 469 MHz range, and will require licensing and coordination with the FCC. It’s $479/10 years for a single frequency license or $579/year for a repeater pair (again, not really relevant to the radio you’re using). If you use the radios without a license (as they come preprogrammed and ready to operate out of the box), will you get away with it? Honestly, the likelihood is pretty decent, especially if you only operate on the Itinerant and low power frequencies. But if the FCC does get a hold of you and decides to levy fines, it’s not a $25 parking ticket… their fines run in the thousands. If you jump on frequencies slotted for an exclusive user in your area and they catch interference from you, they can report it to the FCC, who at that point would send a field unit to identify the source of the disturbance. For ~$50/year, I’d say better to play it safe. If you don’t want to deal with all of that, want to keep it legal, but use a license by rule service, you have some low power 900MHz options, which you probably won’t run into much interference on, but it is shared with ham operators who can operate at higher power levels and ISM equipment. There’s a group of us (licensed ham operators) who like to use Project 25 on the 33 meter band. Family Radio Service is a very well known one. It’s a series of 22 UHF frequencies (was originally 14, but squatters invaded the GMRS exclusive frequencies and the FCC kowtowed to them). Very, very popular… lots of businesses use it, kids playing are often using FRS, it also shares the non-interstitial frequencies with GMRS. You can legally transmit up to two watts in narrow band on the non-interstitial frequencies (Channels 1 - 7 and 15 - 22) and .5 watts in narrow band on the interstitial frequencies (Channels 8 - 14), using a type accepted radio with a non-detachable antenna (I.e., the blister pack radios). Under GMRS rules, you can run up to five watts on the lower non-interstitial frequencies (Channels 1 - 7) and 50 watts with the option to use wide band in the upper non-interstitial frequencies (Channels 15 - 22), plus the ability to use repeaters (paired to the upper non-interstitial frequencies). Licensing of GMRS for business use ended in 1987, though some still have organizational licenses which are grandfathered in, but an individual license covers you and your immediate family members, and that’s $35 for a ten year license. You’re supposed to use a Part 95E type accepted radio, but viable GMRS radios weren’t a thing until recently, so a lot of us took to using Part 90 commercial radios. Or some will use non-certified radios such as the BaoFeng radios (illegally, but I’m not out to be the radio police). The advantage a GMRS specific radio has over an LMR radio is the ability to change PL tones (squelch tones) from the front face. MURS is a bit less common. It’s five VHF frequencies. Very common among big box stores such as Walmart, Costco, Sam’s Club, etc. (to that end, Motorola makes certain submodels of MURS radios specifically for Walmart). Another one where people generally took to using LMR radios, but there are some viable MURS specific options out there, such as the B-Tech MURS-V1. Legal output is two watts, you can use a detachable antenna, allowing you to use an external antenna.

Question: Is it true that good semi-truck drivers float gears? What happens inside the transmission when you do that, and is that bad?
Answer: A good driver will learn their equipment beforehand. Floating gears isn’t difficult, and I wouldn’t consider that as a way of determining if a driver is good or not. If, for example, they jumped into one of the rare Volvos in the US with the 14 speed as it was called and began floating that one, it would be a strike against them because that is a synchromesh transmission. A good driver would learn that before the fact. As far as what happens in the transmission, if done right, nothing out of the ordinary. The gear teeth line up and it goes into gear, else they end up playing ‘grind it til you find it” (which can happen even if you double clutch). On the maintenance side, we prefer that the drivers float rather than double clutch. A number of them learned how to drive in a manual with a regular passenger car, pickup truck, what have you. From that, they got into the habit of pushing the clutch pedal all the way down. Which is normal for a synchromesh transmission. On a unsynchronized transmission (which is typical for trucks in that class of North American manufacture), the transmissions are unsynchronized - the driver does the rev matching to account for the absence of a synchronizer gear. Which is a developed skill of course, but there’s more to driving than just shifting. You might have the smoothest crash box shifting known to man, but if you can’t go down a hill without fading out your brakes, you’re not a good driver. One thing the crash boxes have which a synchromesh transmission doesn’t is a clutch brake. Which is just a friction surface that makes contact when the clutch pedal is fully depressed. It’s for when you’re stopped, so you can get into gear again. If you’re double clutching as you’re going down the road and depressing the clutch pedal all the way, you’re wearing out that clutch brake.

Question: What are the components of a basic air braking system?
Answer: Compressor. This supplies the compressed air to the reservoirs, of course. Reservoirs. The compressed air is potential energy, and the reservoirs are where it is stored. In an FMVSS121 system, it’ll be a dual circuit system with a primary and secondary reservoir. Before those two reservoirs, there may or may not be a third reservoir, known as a wet tank. Air governor. I’ve seen some manufacturers have started going electronic with theee, but they’re traditionally pneumatic. When cutout pressure is released, this will open up and send signal air to the compressor unloading valve and (if equipped) to the air dryer. Air dryer. Includes a cartridge which contains two layers of desiccant for removing moisture and oil from the air discharged from the compressor. That air gets very hot and then cools rapidly, leading to moisture, and small amounts of oil used to live the compressor will get commingled with the pressurized air. You don’t want that going downstream. Most trucks use it, but I’ve encountered some which do not, and instead just use a wet tank. Brake control valve. On a 121 system, for a straight truck, this can either be a PP-1 or PP-DC valve. For a combination air brake vehicle, this may be either a PP-1 and PP-7 valve or an MV3 valve (which is the PP-1, PP-7, and two way check valve in one assembly). Release valves, typically a combination of quick release and relay valves. One thing to clarify from another answer I read, the air going from the foot valve to the relay valve(s) is signal air - it pushes down a plunger to open a direct passage from the reservoir to the brake chamber diaphragm. Brake chambers, of course. Depending on which axle they’re on, they may contain either one or two chambers. Typically, single chambers will be found in the steer axle and lift axles, and dual chambers used on at least one of the drive axles. Piston brakes do exist, which I’ve been told some the UPS fleet uses or used them… I’ve only ever seen them on a New Flyer airport shuttle bus, and they, in my opinion, are shit. Actuation valves, which would consist of your brake pedal (itself an air valve consisting of two chambers and referred to as a pedal valve or treadle valve, depending on the positioning of it) and in the case of combination vehicles, there may also be the trolley valve, which only actuates the trailer brakes. Tractor protection valve, for combination vehicles. This is what keeps the system from dumping air when the hoses aren’t connected to a trailer. I’ve also seen it on some military vehicles and vocational trucks retrofitted to pull an air brake trailer where they won’t install a TPV, and instead have ball valves at the glad hands. A number of our truck tractors have an additional set of glad hands at the rear crossmember which are set up this way, in case they have to use the truck to pull a tag trailer via the pintle hitch rather than a fifth wheel trailer, although we ended this practice in 2020 and now we install a second TPV and an additional valve in the cab rather than using the ball valves. Of course the brake hardware, of which you can get either drum brakes or disc brakes. The disc brakes will consist of the calipers, pads, and rotors (which will be a semi-captive setup where they’re attached to the hub). Drums, you’re dealing with s-cams. Flat cam brakes do exist, but I’ve yet to see them. Wedge brakes are obsolete… we did still have a truck which used them, and ended up getting rid of it because we couldn’t find replacement brake hardware for it and decided it wasn’t worth it to retrofit it to s-cam drum or disc brakes.

Question: What is the operation of a third differential or inter-axle differential?
Answer: A lot of people think an IAD works like a transfer case, where normal operation is one live axle and the other is disengaged. This is incorrect. An IAD supplies power to both axle outputs at all times. When you lock in the IAD, you don’t engage a previously disengaged axle, it locks the outputs so that they’re forced to rotate at the same speed at all times. In an unlocked state, it acts as an open differential, which allows it to account for differences in tire wear between the two axles.

Question: What do you call the extra axle mounted high on the rear of a ready mix truck?
Answer: It’s called a bridge axle, probably made by Strong Arm. Hydraulically raised and lowered, the primary purpose being actually to extend the wheelbase of the truck to the maximum legal length possible (or as close to it as can be achieved), which allows the truck to operate at a heavier weight, ergo, carrying more product. You can call it a tag axle, but a tag axle is just any dead axle which is situated behind the drive axle(s) of a truck (in front, except for the steer axle, is called a pusher), and a tag or pusher axle may be lifting or it may be fixed. Calling it a tag axle is wouldn’t be incorrect, but it falls short. Bridge Master axles seen on some dump trucks serve the same purpose. On this truck, you can see three pusher axles as well, albeit in the raised position. In the US, the acceptable weight a vehicle can operate at is determined by Bridge Law Formula. As the footprint of the vehicle is made larger (thus distributing the weight over a larger area) more weight can be hauled. With the Strong Arm or Bridge Master axles, rather than have the wheelbase be determined by center point of the steer axle to the center point between the two drive axles, it goes center point of the steer axle to the center point of the Strong Arm or Bridge Master axle.

Question: What information do I need to provide when calling for a tow?
Answer: Location of the car is always helpful. Like, really, really helpful. An accurate location at that. I’ll hunt a car down to do a repo, but I really don’t want to be doing that for a roadside tow. Be concise. “It’s a white Chevy Malibu in the Walmart parking lot”. There’s probably five or six of those there. Are you in a parking structure? We would need to know this in order to send a snatch truck to get it. By the way, Tesla owners, since you fucking LOVE to argue about this, wheel lift and wheel dollies is an approved towing method by Tesla, per their website and your own owner’s manual. The only EV I’ve encountered where the OEM was adamant about prohibiting this method was the Porsche Tacan. Anyhow, details matter. Keep in mind as well that, even if you’re submitting the call through an app which does geolocation, those aren’t always pinpoint accurate. If the car is going to be unattended for the tow, whether or not the key is going to be with the car (and where it’s located if it is), and something that can positively identify the car, such as the VIN number, license plate number, if you have a “Je suis Charlie” sticker with Charles Manson’s face on it, that could help confirm it’s the right car. Your silver Hyundai Elantra looks just like the other three or four which will inevitably be in the parking lot when we arrive. If something happened like, say, the front end of the car got t-boned and now the front crossmember is sticking out well past where the front of the car would normally be, that’s a good one. If you have flat tires, how many and which ones would be helpful to know beforehand. One front tire flat on a Honda Civic? Not a problem. Four flat tires and you’re going to try getting them repaired? Better to send a rollback because flat tires tend to sag and drag when you dolly them. If your car is laying on its roof, be sure to mention that, especially if you’re using AAA for the tow. During the plague years, I worked weekends for a AAA motor club towing company. For many people there, it was their first towing job, and the training they offered wasn’t that comprehensive, ergo, a majority of the rollback drivers did not know how to upright a car. Of our wheel lift fleet, most of the trucks were autoloaders - snatch trucks - with a single line, no rings to attach a snatch block to, and they didn’t carry a stiff leg setup with them. Of course, in the absence of rings and if I wasn’t going to use a stiff leg, I kept a 2” long 6x4 which I’d wrap a chain around, run that between the duals, then attach a snatch block that. But anyhow. If someone decided to ventilate their head with a shotgun or there was a fatality accident and there’s blood and gore all over the place, that’s good to know. Because some people don’t have the stomach for it. Me, I’m always down for some cheap gore, but not everyone running a tow truck is. But this is more of a gripe I’d air with IAA/Copart and a County Sheriffs Office here in NC.

Question: What is a Non-CDL Class C License in the state of Colorado?
Answer: In Colorado, Class C is your basic operator permit without restrictions. In non-exempt use, it allows you to operate any Category C single vehicle or combination which doesn’t not require a CDL. The only ways a Category C vehicle requires a CDL is if it’s being used in a manner which requires an endorsement that can only be had on a CDL. For example, a shuttle bus on an Econoline E450 chassis. It doesn’t require a CDL on account of weight, but a bus designed to seat more than 15 people (including the driver) requires a passenger endorsement and that only be had on a CDL. Or if you were driving a stake bed truck on a one ton pickup chassis, that wouldn’t require a CDL. But let’s say that truck was being used to transport welding gases and the quantity it transported required hazardous material placards to be displayed. You would be required to have a hazmat endorsement to operate that vehicle, and that endorsement can only be had on a CDL. Your category C vehicles include… Exempt use is a whole new can of worms to open, and it tends to allow you to operate vehicles which would require a CDL in non-exempt use, but the particulars of their use makes them exempt. For example, you’re in the Army Reserve and you operate an M915 line haul tractor, which is a militarized Freightliner truck tractor. That falls under the military exemption and you as a service member in the course of your duties would not need a CDL to operate it on public roadways, though you would need to be licensed through your branch (in the case of the Army, the military driver’s license is a DA Form 348). First responders aren’t required to have a CDL, though some jurisdictions impose that requirement anyhow. Stuff like that. But yeah, non-CDL Class C is your basic, unrestricted drivers license in Colorado. And it doesn’t mean they’d reject you if you had a Class A, B, or C CDL, they just posted the minimum requirement.
